name: Xiao-qing-long-tang (Chinese herbal formula; sho-seiryu-to in Japanese, so-cheong-ryong-tang in Korean)
short: Case reports: pneumonitis (one with lung bleeding), pneumonia with eosinophilia. Most-reported formula in Taiwan herbal reports. Contains ephedra, licorice. Lab: aristolochic compounds in a granule.
text: Names: abstracts give Sho-seiryu-to and Shoseiryuto as names of Xiao-Qing-Long-Tang in Japanese (Kampo) medicine, and So-Cheong-Ryong-Tang, also known as Sho-seiryo-to, as a name used in traditional Korean medicine; one abstract states that it contains eight herbs, including ephedra (Ephedra sinica), and others that it contains Ephedrae Herba, licorice (Glycyrrhizae Radix) and Schisandra fruit. Lungs (case reports): a 78-year-old man taking it for allergic rhinitis developed pneumonitis with diffuse bleeding into the lungs (alveolar haemorrhage), which resolved after it was stopped and corticosteroids were given; a 67-year-old man given it with other drugs for a cold developed drug-induced interstitial pneumonia, with a positive lymphocyte stimulation test for the formula and negative tests for the other drugs; and a 25-year-old woman developed pneumonia with low blood oxygen and a marked rise in eosinophils three days after taking it, with a positive lymphocyte stimulation test, improving after it was stopped and steroids were given. In another case, a man who had taken it with amoxicillin and acetaminophen developed eosinophilic pneumonia, and a provocation test showed that amoxicillin caused the reaction. In that case the lymphocyte stimulation test was positive for a different drug (acetaminophen), and a review of one hospital department's admission records from 1979 to 1999, covering liver injury suspected to be related to Kampo medicines, found that most patients judged definitely unrelated had a positive lymphocyte transformation test for the suspect Kampo medicine, which the authors say suggests the test may be unreliable for diagnosing Kampo-related liver injury. A 2017 literature review of 73 published patients (59 articles) with pneumonitis caused by Japanese herbal medicines in general (other formulas were the most frequent causes, and the abstract does not name this one) found that 26 (36%) recovered after simply stopping the medicine, while the rest needed immunosuppressive treatment; 13 (18%) needed mechanical ventilation and 3 (4%) died. Reports: in Taiwan's adverse-reaction reporting system for herbal medicines (2,079 reports, 1998 to 2016), Xiao-Qing-Long-Tang was the most commonly reported herbal formula; reports of this kind cannot show cause or frequency. Trials, taken by mouth: a 2022 meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials in allergic rhinitis describes the formula as well tolerated; in a multicentre placebo-controlled Korean trial in adults with perennial allergic rhinitis, no serious adverse events and no changes in safety assessments were seen; in a 46-person crossover study in cedar pollen allergy, no significant side effects were detected; in a 60-person placebo-controlled trial in people with atopic dermatitis and respiratory disorders, including children, no participant showed remarkable abnormal signs in the safety evaluation; and in a 124-person randomized trial in a flare-up of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in which the formula, as a decoction, was added to conventional Western treatment, no severe adverse reactions such as liver or kidney dysfunction occurred and no adverse reactions associated with the decoction were observed, while a meta-analysis of 38 such trials found no difference in adverse events but called its safety uncertain. Ephedra, licorice and potassium: in 6 healthy volunteers, ephedrine and related substances banned in sport appeared in the urine after a single dose, below the permitted value, and a further three-day test gave a positive urine ephedrine result (the abstract does not say in whom). A 2022 review of Kampo medicines in general (not this formula) lists sympathomimetic symptoms caused by ephedra and pseudoaldosteronism caused by licorice among adverse effects linked to overdose. In Japan's national adverse-event reports for prescription Kampo formulas in general (4,232 events, July 2003 to March 2018; the abstract does not name this formula), the largest categories were liver injury (1,193 events) and lung injury (1,177), and about 70% of these were suspected to be caused by formulas containing Scutellaria root (the cited abstracts do not say whether this formula contains it); pseudoaldosteronism, attributed to licorice, was reported 889 times and included several events related to muscle injury, heart failure and arrhythmia, and about 35% of drug-eruption events were suspected to be caused by formulas containing ephedra. An analysis of Japanese reports of pseudoaldosteronism with 148 Kampo formulas (the abstract does not name this formula) found diuretic use among the associated factors, and its authors advise careful follow-up during long-term use of licorice-containing formulas in people with several such factors. A laboratory study of 25 licorice-containing Kampo extracts found that Schisandra fruit in this formula drastically decreased the extraction of glycyrrhizin (the licorice constituent that can cause pseudoaldosteronism), and that glycyrrhizin content correlated with reported pseudoaldosteronism across the 25 extracts. PubMed searches found no report of liver injury, pseudoaldosteronism or low potassium naming this formula. Aristolochic acid (laboratory data): a 2023 laboratory study measured aristolochic acids I and II and a third compound, abbreviated ALI (the abstract does not expand it), in herbs and Chinese patent medicines, and gave the combined amount of the three only as a range across six samples listed in descending order, with Xiaoqinglong granules (a granule preparation of the formula) last; the abstract gives no figure for this product alone and does not say whether it harmed the kidneys of the zebrafish larvae tested. A Taiwanese study describes aristolochic acid as nephrotoxic (harmful to the kidneys) and carcinogenic. No report of kidney injury in people naming this formula was found. Pregnancy: no pregnancy-outcome data for this formula were found; a Japanese database study reports that it was among the formulas most prescribed during pregnancy and says further research is needed on the relationship between Kampo use in pregnancy and adverse events in infants. Interactions: in 37 healthy volunteers given the formula for 7 days, the activity of five drug-metabolising enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP3A, xanthine oxidase and NAT2) did not change, and the authors conclude that it is unlikely to cause interactions with medicines cleared mainly by those pathways. Diuretics are named only as a factor associated with licorice-related pseudoaldosteronism across Kampo formulas, not as an interaction studied with this formula.
